Part 1 — Welcome and introductions

Who we are, how this course works, and the one rule: no new theory - integration. · Lecture 0:00-0:11 · Activity 0:11-0:15

Slide 5 / 55 Part 1 — Welcome and introductions◀ 4 6 ▶

1Lecture notes (0:00-0:11)

Opening (0:00-0:02)

Slide 6 / 55 Welcome — and now you: name, program, one routine◀ 5 7 ▶

Good morning, and welcome to CS (Computer Science) 251, Integrative Project 1. My name is Asen Grozdanov; most people call me Cyber. Before I taught, I spent about twenty-five years working in the IT (Information Technology) industry, and that is exactly the direction of this course: from the industry to the classroom. In industry, nobody hands you a problem labelled "statistics" or "economics" or "programming". You receive a business problem, and you have to decide which knowledge answers which part of it. That decision is what you will practise for fifteen Fridays.

Introductions (0:02-0:06)

Now you. Each student, in one breath: your name, your program, and one routine you would love to never do again.

A routine is a task that repeats on a regular schedule - every day, every week - and that follows more or less the same steps each time. Checking a mailbox every morning is a routine. Writing the same status report every Friday is a routine. Registering for a course once a year is not a routine; it is an event. Keep that distinction, because the whole project is about routines: the ones that can be automated, and the ones that cannot.

While you speak, I will write your routines on the board. By the end of the round we will have a list of twenty or thirty routines; several of them will look very much like the routines of the company we are going to work for.

Expectations, both ways (0:06-0:09)

Slide 7 / 55 Expectations — both ways◀ 6 8 ▶

What I expect from you, every week:

  • You attend the Friday session; it is one hour of lecture and two hours of team work, and the team work cannot happen without you.
  • You submit the week's Brick - the one deliverable of the week - by Thursday 23:59 before the next class, on the LMS (Learning Management System) and on GitHub.
  • You commit code to the team repository every week. Commits from every member count; a team with one person typing and two people watching is visible in the history.
  • You ask questions. If I do not know the answer, I will write it on the Parking Lot and answer it next Friday.

What you can expect from me:

  • The same rhythm every Friday, so you always know what comes next.
  • A grade for every Brick within a week - complete, partial or missing, plus one comment.
  • One specific, true, positive sentence to every team, every week.

How this course works - no new theory (0:09-0:11)

Slide 8 / 55 The one rule: no new theory — integration◀ 7 9 ▶

This is the sentence to remember: this course adds no new theory. Everything you need was taught in three courses you have already taken: Principles of Microeconomics, Introduction to OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) in Python, and Statistics. What is new is the integration: using those three kinds of knowledge together, on one real problem, until you have a working tool and a recommendation a business owner can act on.

The official syllabus describes an integrative project as a sustained period of independent study and research, combined with interaction with other students, starting from a real-world business problem and leading to a research-based solution. We will come back to that definition in Part 2. For now, keep three words: one problem, three courses, one team.

One last thing before the activity. Every material you receive in this course - this page, the demos, the figures, the datasets - is educational material of the Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub, and its use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (version 2.0). The link is at the top and at the bottom of this page. Read section 2 (acceptance), section 4 (intellectual property) and section 18 (academic integrity) this week. The university's own policies - code of conduct, attendance, academic honesty, resit - apply in full and are linked from the official syllabus.

Integration

Brick

5Real-life example - Alex's first day in the time log

Slide 11 / 55 Real-life example — Alex's first day in the time log◀ 10 12 ▶
Slide 13 / 55 The privacy rule — a time log is personal data◀ 12 14 ▶

Task. Alex is a first-year CS (Computer Science) student. On Friday, September 25, 2026, Alex records every study and work routine of the day as one row each - date, routine, minutes, interruptions - then totals the minutes per routine, finds the routine that took the most time, and writes the rows as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

How it relates to this part. In the introductions you named one routine; the time log turns routines into data. From today, every student is a pilot user of the project and keeps a personal 14-day time log (two minutes a day). The file data/timelog_<initials>.csv with at least five rows per member is a deliverable of Brick 1 (due Thursday, October 1), and in Brick 4 (October 22) you will analyse your own log with the same statistics you apply to the studio's data.

Privacy rule. A time log is personal data. It stays in the private team repository, anonymised: routine names, minutes and timestamps only - no names of other people, no message contents. Nothing personal ever reaches a public web page. See the Cyber.SoHo Notice, sections 6.7 and 20, and the privacy laws summarised in section 8.3.

Demo 1 - Time Log Builder. Task: Build one day of a personal time log row by row, total the minutes per routine, find the routine with the most minutes, and produce the CSV text that Brick 1 asks for. Relation to the lecture: Part 1 (the routine you named) and the 14-day time log that starts today; feeds Brick 1 (log started, >= 5 rows) and Brick 4 (your log analysed).
Show the code — every line is preceded by a comment that explains what it does and why

Step by step — what happens when it runs

  1. Press Start: the demo creates an empty log with the four columns of Brick 1 (date, routine, minutes, interruptions).
  2. Steps 2 to 7 add Alex's six rows one at a time. Watch the table on the left and the bar chart above it: each row adds minutes to the bar of its routine.
  3. Row 5 is a second run of email_check. One routine can run several times a day; each run is its own row, and the bar for email_check grows from 25 to 35 minutes.
  4. Step 8 groups the rows by routine name and totals the minutes (this is the same grouping Brick 4 does with Python's collections.defaultdict).
  5. Step 9 finds the largest total - lecture_notes, 50 minutes - and colours that bar rust.
  6. Step 10 counts interruptions per routine; in Brick 4 you will ask whether more interruptions go with more minutes (correlation).
  7. Step 11 writes the CSV text: one header line, then one line per row, commas between values. Press Download CSV to save it.
  8. Press Pause at any moment: the execution log on the right keeps every step so it can be discussed; Start resumes from the same step. Next step runs one step at a time. Restart clears everything.

The demo runs entirely in your browser: no internet, no libraries, no tracking. Reuse for study is permitted; redistribution and commercial use are not — Cyber.SoHo Notice §4, §4.3, §6.6.

Part 2 — What is an integrative project?

The consulting habit - problem, evidence, recommendation - and why three courses are needed together. · Lecture 0:15-0:26 · Activity 0:26-0:30

Slide 15 / 55 Part 2 — What is an integrative project?◀ 14 16 ▶

1Lecture notes (0:15-0:26)

The definition (0:15-0:18)

Slide 16 / 55 The definition, word by word (1/2)◀ 15 17 ▶
Slide 17 / 55 The definition, word by word (2/2)◀ 16 18 ▶

Let us read the official definition slowly, because every word in it is a requirement.

An integrative project provides a sustained period of independent study and research, combined with interaction with other students. Two things at once: you work independently on research, and you work with a team.

It starts with a real-world business problem, provided by the instructor or by an industrial partner. This year the problem is provided by me, and the business is a small Montréal consultancy. You will meet it in Part 4.

Then a research-based solution is sought, integrating the knowledge acquired in previous courses, aiming to reproduce real-world consulting activities. Three requirements in one sentence: the solution must be based on research, not on opinion; it must integrate what you already know; and the whole exercise reproduces what a consultant does for a client.

And finally: the course does not include additional theoretical content. We said it in Part 1. The syllabus even gives the example of this year's project: a Python application that automates the routine work of a small company, records real usage data, and applies statistics and microeconomics to that data to make business decisions.

The consulting habit: problem, evidence, recommendation (0:18-0:22)

Slide 18 / 55 The consulting habit: problem, evidence, recommendation◀ 17 19 ▶
Slide 19 / 55 The research side: from the problem to the research questions◀ 18 20 ▶

A consulting engagement is a contract in which a client asks an outside expert to analyse a problem and recommend a decision. The client does not want a lecture; the client wants to know what to do. So consultants work in a fixed order, and we will keep that order in every Brick:

  1. Problem. State what the client is actually asking. Not "e-mail is annoying", but "which routine should we automate first, how much time would it save, and is a free assistant good enough?"
  2. Evidence. Collect data and analyse it. Evidence is what makes a solution research-based: numbers that come from observations, computed with methods you can name and defend.
  3. Recommendation. Turn the evidence into a decision the client can act on, with its expected impact and its risk.

Our textbook, Leedy and Ormrod's Practical Research: Planning and Design, describes the research side of this order: a research problem is split into sub-problems, each sub-problem becomes a research question (abbreviated RQ), and data is collected to answer each question. In Class 2 you will write your own problem statement and three research questions. Today, just recognise the shape.

Why three courses together (0:22-0:26)

Slide 20 / 55 Why three courses together◀ 19 21 ▶

Here is the same business question split into its three sub-problems, and notice that each one belongs to a different course:

  • What is an hour of staff time worth, and what does automation cost? That is Principles of Microeconomics: opportunity cost (the value of the next-best use of a resource), marginal benefit versus marginal cost (what one more unit of automation gains against what it costs), fixed and variable costs, and break-even (the point at which the benefit equals the cost).
  • What does the time log actually show? That is Statistics: the mean (the sum divided by the count), the median (the middle value of the sorted data), the standard deviation (abbreviated SD: a measure of how spread out the values are), a correlation (whether two quantities move together), and a before/after comparison of a process change.
  • How do we automate a routine and measure the saving? That is OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) in Python: classes (templates that bundle data with the operations on that data), objects (instances of a class), and the modules of the standard library that read files and compute statistics.

None of the three answers the owner's question on its own. Economics without data is a guess; statistics without a tool is a spreadsheet nobody maintains; a program without economics automates the wrong routine. The three-circle diagram on the screen shows the intersection: Microeconomics ∩ Python ∩ Statistics is where CS 251 lives. Every Brick sits in that intersection, and so does every question of the Mid-Term.

One more definition, because we will use it constantly: JARVIS is the name of the assistant you will build - a name, not an abbreviation. By January, JARVIS must log and automate routine work, measure the time it saves with statistics, price that time with microeconomics, and recommend what to automate first and whether the free tier is enough. That sentence is the first outcome of today's class: be able to say it without notes.

2Terms to learn in this part

Integrative project
Independent study and research with a team, starting from a real business problem, leading to a research-based solution that integrates previous courses and reproduces consulting work.
Consulting engagement
A contract in which a client asks an outside expert to analyse a problem and recommend a decision.
Evidence
Numbers obtained from observations and computed with methods you can name and defend; what makes a solution research-based.
Research question (RQ)
A precise question, derived from a sub-problem, that data can answer.
Opportunity cost
The value of the next-best use of a resource - for staff time, the work that could have been done instead.
Median
The middle value of the sorted data (the average of the two middle values when the count is even).

5Real-life example - E-mail triage at Boréal Studio, from a complaint to a recommendation

Slide 24 / 55 Real-life example — e-mail triage at Boréal Studio◀ 23 25 ▶

Task. The owner of Boréal Studio says: "E-mail triage eats our mornings. Should we automate it first, and is a free assistant good enough?" Walk that complaint through the chain: state the problem; collect evidence (seven days of triage minutes for one staff member: 62, 35, 30, 33, 40, 31, 38); compute the mean and the median (Statistics); convert the typical day into a monthly cost with the three given numbers (Microeconomics: minutes ÷ 60 × 28 $/h × 20 working days × 5 staff ≈ 1 633 $); note that the same computation will be one Python method (OOP, Object-Oriented Programming); and write the recommendation in four parts: finding, evidence, decision, risk.

How it relates to this part. This is the consulting habit applied once, end to end, with each of the three courses supplying one piece. The same chain is the structure of Brick 2 (problem statement and research questions RQ1-RQ3, due October 8), Brick 3 (routine cost and opportunity cost, October 15) and Brick 4 (mean, median and the honest "typical day", October 22). The four-part recommendation pattern returns in Brick 7 and in the Product Defense.

Show the code — every line is preceded by a comment that explains what it does and why

Step by step — what happens when it runs

  1. Step 1 states the owner's problem in her own words and highlights the Problem box.
  2. Step 2 splits the problem into three sub-problems, one per course - the Venn circles are still dark.
  3. Step 3 collects the evidence: seven daily durations appear as dots; the Monday value (62 minutes) is far from the others.
  4. Steps 4 and 5 compute the mean (38.4) and the median (35) and draw both lines; the Statistics circle lights up. The median is the honest typical day because one value is extreme.
  5. Steps 6 and 7 convert the typical day into a monthly cost (about 1 633 $ for five people) and name the opportunity cost; the Microeconomics circle lights up.
  6. Step 8 shows that the computation becomes a method, EconEngine.routine_cost(...); the Python circle lights up - all three circles are lit at once.
  7. Steps 9 to 12 write the recommendation line by line: finding, evidence, decision, risk. The Recommendation box is highlighted.
  8. Use Pause after step 5 to discuss mean versus median, and after step 8 to discuss why no single course was enough. Download figure saves the diagram as SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) or PNG (Portable Network Graphics) for your notes.

Part 3 — Course map, grading and the Brick system

Fifteen Fridays in four phases, the 1:2:2 rhythm, 30/30/40, and why every Brick is a page of your Mid-Term. · Lecture 0:30-0:41 · Activity 0:41-0:45

1Lecture notes (0:30-0:41)

The map: fifteen Fridays, four phases (0:30-0:33)

Slide 29 / 55 Six dates to memorise — and two that matter soon◀ 28 30 ▶

Look at the timeline (Figure 3). We meet fifteen Fridays, from September 25, 2026 to January 22, 2027, with a winter break from December 21 to January 8. The Fridays are grouped in four phases:

  • Phase 1 - Analysis, Classes 1 to 4 (September 25 to October 16): understand the problem, write the requirements, refresh microeconomics and statistics on the real data. Deliverable: the Project Proposal and Requirement Analysis - Bricks 1 to 4.
  • Phase 2 - Midterm phase, Classes 5 to 9 (October 23 to November 20): design the software, build the first working version, present it (the Alpha Demo on November 6), review, and sit the Mid-Term on November 20.
  • Phase 3 - Development and Test, Classes 10 to 13 (November 27 to December 18): tests, error resolution, going live, results and charts, the report draft. Three of those Fridays - December 4, 11 and 18 - are Project Sprints: supervised work sessions with no lecture, where teams work through a written brief.
  • Phase 4 - Final, Classes 14 and 15 (January 15 and 22): the dress rehearsal and the Product Defense.

Six dates to memorise today: November 13 (Mid-Term Review), November 20 (Mid-Term), December 4, 11 and 18 (Sprints), January 15 (Final Review) and January 22 (Final). Two more that matter soon: October 22, when Phase 1 closes with Brick 4, and November 6, the Alpha Demo.

The rhythm: 1 : 2 : 2 (0:33-0:35)

Slide 30 / 55 The rhythm: 1 : 2 : 2 — every Friday has the same shape◀ 29 31 ▶

Every Friday has the same shape, and that predictability is deliberate.

  • 1 hour of lecture, split into three or four short parts of eleven to fifteen minutes, each followed by a three-to-five-minute activity - a visualization, a short practical exercise, flash-cards, a quiz, or a zen break. Nobody sits through sixty minutes of talking.
  • 2 hours of in-class workshop: your team works on the week's Brick; the last fifteen minutes are the checkpoint, when every team shows the day's result on screen for thirty to sixty seconds.
  • 2 hours at home: finish the Brick, read a short extract of Leedy and Ormrod, and write your Weekly Progress Report.

The syllabus counts three credit hours as 135 to 180 total study hours for the semester; the rhythm above is how those hours are distributed.

Grading: 30 / 30 / 40 (0:35-0:38)

Slide 31 / 55 Grading: 30 / 30 / 40◀ 30 32 ▶
  • Continuous Course Assessments - 30 %. Twelve Bricks at 2.5 % each. Each Brick is graded Complete (2.5), Partial (1.25) or Missing (0), plus one comment. The continuous assessment also counts your weekly progress reports, your commits and your peer-review participation, as the syllabus says.
  • Midterm Assessment - 30 %. Friday, November 20: a two-hour, individual, computational and application exam. Part A is computational (costs, break-even, payback, mean, median, standard deviation, correlation); Part B is application (complete or fix a Python method, read a design diagram, write requirements and research questions). The allowed materials will be announced in Class 5; the plan is one handwritten Formula Card and one handwritten Design Card.
  • Final Assessment - 40 %. Friday, January 22: a Product Defense - a live demonstration of the working assistant, a public presentation with guests, and the submission of the technical report and the codebase the day before, January 21 at 23:59.

Letter grades follow the syllabus scale: 93-100 A, 90-92 A-, 87-89 B+, 83-86 B, 80-82 B-, 77-79 C+, 73-76 C, 70-72 C-, 60-69 D, 59 and below F.

The Brick system (0:38-0:41)

Slide 33 / 55 The Brick system — twelve weeks, twelve Bricks, one project◀ 32 34 ▶
Slide 34 / 55 Brick rules — in five lines◀ 33 35 ▶

A Brick is the one deliverable of the week: a document, a script, a diagram, a set of tests. Twelve Bricks, twelve weeks. The Bricks are not separate homework: they assemble into JARVIS, and nothing is thrown away - not even the Mid-Term, whose corrected Part A becomes the first draft of your report's Results section.

The one fact that decides the Mid-Term: the exam is written on the JARVIS basis - the same routines data, the same formulas you coded in Bricks 3 and 4, the same design you drew in Brick 5. Every Brick you submit on time is a page of your own preparation; every gap is a gap in the exam. Bricks 1 to 7 must be complete and submitted by Thursday, November 12.

The rules, in five lines:

  1. Every Brick is due Thursday 23:59 before the next class: files on the LMS (Learning Management System), code on GitHub, tagged where the class page says so.
  2. One team submission per Brick, plus one individual Weekly Progress Report per student - ten lines, ten minutes: what I did, what the team delivered, what I will do next, blockers, hours spent, one thing I learned.
  3. Commits from every member count. Git activity is part of the continuous assessment.
  4. The late policy is announced on the LMS. A missing Brick must still be submitted: the Mid-Term and the report are built on it.
  5. Cite your sources - code, documentation pages and AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance included - in APA (American Psychological Association) 7 style. Reused code without a citation is an academic-honesty case under the university's policy and under section 18 of the Cyber.SoHo Notice.

APA (American Psychological Association) 7

5Real-life example - Maya's grade path through the fifteen Fridays

Slide 35 / 55 Real-life example — Maya's grade path◀ 34 36 ▶

Task. Maya is a student in this course. Compute her final grade week by week: twelve Bricks (2.5 points each when complete, 1.25 when partial, 0 when missing), then the Mid-Term (score out of 100 × 0.30), then the Final (score out of 100 × 0.40), and read the letter on the syllabus scale. Compare three paths: every Brick complete; two Bricks missing; four partial Bricks with weaker exams.

How it relates to this part. The grade is the 30/30/40 rule turned into arithmetic, so the example makes the rule concrete. It also shows what one missing Brick costs: with the same exam results, two missing Bricks turn a B+ into a B-, before counting the Mid-Term questions that were written on those Bricks. The habit of turning a written rule into a computation is exactly what Brick 3 (economic formulas → EconEngine methods) and Brick 6 (the console Reporter that prints one line per routine) ask for.

Part 4 — Meet the client and the toolbox

Boréal Studio's problem, the dataset, the three given numbers, the tools, and the JARVIS loop. · Lecture 0:45-0:56 · Activity 0:56-1:00

Slide 39 / 55 Part 4 — Meet the client and the toolbox◀ 38 40 ▶

1Lecture notes (0:45-0:56)

The client (0:45-0:48)

Slide 40 / 55 The client — Boréal Studio, Montréal◀ 39 41 ▶

Boréal Studio is a five-person consultancy in Montréal. It is a teaching case: the company is fictional, the data is synthetic, and that is deliberate - no real person's working hours are exposed in this course. The studio loses hours every week to routines nobody was hired for: triaging e-mail (sorting the mailbox and deciding what needs an answer), writing the daily report, scheduling meetings, checking invoices, preparing stand-up notes (the short notes for the daily team meeting) and posting on social media. Six routines, five people, fourteen working days of timed data.

The owner's question, in her words: "Which of these routines should we automate first, how much time would it really save, and is a free assistant good enough - or should we pay for one?" She wants a tool that works, not a lecture.

You are also part of the case: from today, every student is a pilot user who keeps a personal 14-day time log, as we said in Part 1.

The dataset (0:48-0:51)

Slide 41 / 55 The dataset — one row per routine run◀ 40 42 ▶

The file is boreal_routines_2026.csv, a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file: plain text, one line per record, values separated by commas, with a header line that names the columns. It has about 420 rows: 14 working days × 5 staff × about 6 routines, one row per routine run. The nine columns:

Column Meaning Python type
date The day of the run, written yyyy-mm-dd datetime.date
staff_id An anonymous code for the person (S1 ... S5) str
routine The name of the routine (email_triage, daily_report, ...) str
category The family of the routine (communication, reporting, planning, finance, marketing) str
start_hour The hour the run started, 0-23 int
minutes How long the run took int
interruptions How many times the person was interrupted during the run int
tool How the run was done: manual, template or jarvis str
done Whether the run was completed: 1 yes, 0 no bool (stored as 0/1)

The data contains two deliberate events you will discover with statistics: a process change (a report template introduced on day 8) and a pilot automation (assistant-triaged e-mail from day 10). They exist so that a before/after comparison and a correlation can be computed honestly. Teams may propose their own real small-business data instead - anonymised, approved by me in Class 2; if you do, section 7.9 of the Cyber.SoHo Notice on work involving a real organization applies.

The three given numbers (0:51-0:52)

Slide 42 / 55 The three given numbers◀ 41 43 ▶

Three numbers are given separately, because they are inputs to the economics, not columns of the data:

  1. The hourly value of staff time: 28 $ per hour, a loaded cost - salary plus the employer's overhead per hour worked.
  2. The price of a paid assistant tier: 20 $ per user per month - a fixed cost per period.
  3. The free API quota - API stands for Application Programming Interface, the way a program talks to another program over the network. Free tiers change; the number and the date it was read are posted on the LMS (Learning Management System), and you will record both in your economics notes.

The toolbox - Python only (0:52-0:54)

Slide 43 / 55 The toolbox — Python only◀ 42 44 ▶
  • Python 3.12 or newer, with its standard library: the modules csv (reads and writes CSV files), sqlite3 (a small database engine that stores everything in one file), statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, correlation) and dataclasses (classes that hold data with less code).
  • VS Code (Visual Studio Code), an editor with a Python extension; an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) if you prefer that word.
  • A virtual environment (python -m venv .venv): a private copy of Python for one project, so that the packages of one project never conflict with another. pip (the Package Installer for Python) installs packages into it.
  • Git and GitHub: Git records every version of your files; GitHub hosts the private team repository, runs GitHub Actions (scripts that run automatically on a schedule or on every push) and serves GitHub Pages (a public web page generated from the repository).
  • pytest (the test framework we will use from Class 10) and matplotlib (the charting library for the report).
  • The LMS for submissions, and the textbook: Leedy and Ormrod, Practical Research: Planning and Design, 12th edition.

No Java is needed anywhere in this course.

The JARVIS loop and the offline rule (0:54-0:56)

Slide 44 / 55 The JARVIS loop — and the offline fallback rule◀ 43 45 ▶

JARVIS - the name of our assistant - works in a loop of five stages, and the diagram (Figure 4) shows it on one line:

  1. Request - a user types a sentence, for example log 25 min email_triage.
  2. Intent - a provider turns the sentence into a structured intent: a name (log_time) and arguments (minutes = 25, routine = email_triage). The first provider is offline: rules and regular expressions (patterns that match text), deterministic, no key, no network.
  3. Tool - the agent looks up the intent name in its table of tools and selects one (LogTimeTool).
  4. Result - the tool runs and changes the store: a new entry in the tiny database file data/jarvis.db.
  5. Log - the run is recorded: timestamp, request, intent, tool, provider, success, milliseconds. That log is JARVIS's own dataset, and in December it feeds the "time saved" numbers.

The offline fallback rule: JARVIS must run with no API key and no network. Tests, the exam and the demos must never depend on the internet. The API provider you connect in Class 10 (a free LLM (Large Language Model) tier) is an upgrade that drops into the same loop, never a dependency.

That is the whole toolbox. In the workshop you will install it, create the team repository, run hello_jarvis.py on the dataset, and write the charter.

2Terms to learn in this part

CSV (Comma-Separated Values)
A plain-text file with one line per record, values separated by commas, and a header line naming the columns.
Loaded cost
The cost of one hour of work including salary and the employer's overhead - here 28 $ per hour.
API (Application Programming Interface)
The way one program talks to another program, here over the network; a free tier limits how many requests are allowed.
Virtual environment
A private copy of Python for one project, created with python -m venv .venv, so that packages of different projects never conflict.
Intent
The structured form of a request: an intent name plus its arguments, produced by a provider.
Offline fallback
The rule that JARVIS must work with no API key and no network; the offline provider uses rules and regular expressions.

Slide 46 / 55 Example — JARVIS hears “log 25 min email_triage”◀ 45 47 ▶

Task. Read the day-1 preview of the studio dataset (thirty rows: five staff × six routines), print the first three rows the way hello_jarvis.py will, group the minutes per routine to answer the activity question, then process one request - log 25 min email_triage - through the five stages of the loop with the offline provider, and record the run.

The same steps are Brick 1 (hello_jarvis.py reads the first three rows with the csv module and you log your first routine), Brick 5 (loader.py parses every row safely and skips bad rows) and Brick 7 (the OfflineProvider, the Tool base class and the Agent - the Alpha Demo of November 6).

Same slide Slide 46 — Example — JARVIS hears “log 25 min email_triage”
Demo 4 - JARVIS Loop Simulator. Task: Read the day-1 preview of boreal_routines_2026.csv, find the routine with the most minutes, then run one request through request -> intent -> tool -> result -> log with the offline provider. Relation to the lecture: Part 4 (the client, the dataset, the three given numbers, the toolbox, the JARVIS loop); feeds Brick 1 (hello_jarvis.py), Brick 5 (loader.py) and Brick 7 (OfflineProvider and Agent).
Show the code — every line is preceded by a comment that explains what it does and why

Step by step — what happens when it runs

  1. Step 1 reads the file text (thirty-one lines) and prints the first three rows in the preview box - the output of hello_jarvis.py in Brick 1.
  2. Step 2 parses the header into the nine column names; step 3 turns every line into a record and converts minutes and interruptions to integers.
  3. Step 4 groups the minutes per routine and draws the bar chart; step 5 answers the activity question - email_triage, 198 minutes on day 1, and the longest single run (S3, 48 minutes).
  4. Step 6 receives the request text (you can edit it before pressing Start); the Request box turns rust.
  5. Step 7 applies the offline rule - the regular expression ^log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)$ - and builds the intent log_time with its arguments. Try a sentence that does not match: JARVIS answers 'I did not understand' instead of crashing.
  6. Step 8 looks up the tool table and selects LogTimeTool; step 9 runs it and appends the entry (the store grows to 31 records).
  7. Step 10 writes the run record (timestamp, request, intent, tool, provider = offline, ok, ms) and prints JARVIS's reply.
  8. Step 11 closes the loop and restates the offline rule. Download day-1 preview (CSV) gives you the thirty rows to try the activity command on.

9Self-check quiz

No slide The quiz runs in this page only — formative, never graded.
FORMATIVEThis quiz is formative, not summative: it is a self-check. It is not graded, it is not recorded, and it does not count towards your final grade. Four MCQ (Multiple-Choice Questions: one right answer out of four) and two MSQ (Multiple-Select Questions: several right answers out of six).

  1. 1. MCQ Approximately how many rows does boreal_routines_2026.csv contain, and why? (1 right answer expected)

    Hint: One row per routine run.
    Right answer: B. 14 days × 5 people × about 6 routines ≈ 420 runs, one row each.

  2. 2. MCQ What is the hourly value of staff time given for the project? (1 right answer expected)

    Hint: It is a loaded cost - salary plus overhead.
    Right answer: B. 28 $/h is the loaded hourly value; 20 $ is the monthly price per user of the paid assistant tier, not an hourly rate.

  3. 3. MCQ Which sequence is the JARVIS loop? (1 right answer expected)

    Hint: It starts with a sentence typed by a user and ends with a record of the run.
    Right answer: A. A request is turned into an intent by a provider, the agent selects a tool, the tool produces a result, and the run is logged.

  4. 4. MCQ What must JARVIS do when there is no API key and no network? (1 right answer expected)

    Hint: Demos, tests and the exam must never depend on the internet.
    Right answer: C. The offline fallback is a non-functional requirement of the project: the offline provider is the default and the API provider is a drop-in upgrade.

  5. 5. MSQ Which of the following are columns of the dataset? (3 right answers expected)

    Hint: Nine columns, none of them financial or personal.
    Right answers: A, B, C. minutes, interruptions and tool are three of the nine columns. Salaries are not in the data (the hourly value is given separately), and no message contents or credentials ever enter the dataset.

  6. 6. MSQ Which tools are part of the Python-only toolbox of the project? (3 right answers expected)

    Hint: No Java is needed anywhere in this course.
    Right answers: A, B, C. Python 3.12+, Git/GitHub and pytest are in the toolbox (with VS Code, matplotlib and the standard library). The JDK (Java Development Kit) and JUnit belong to Java, which is not used, and the analysis is done in Python, not in spreadsheet macros.

In-class workshop (1:00-3:00) - Brick 1 "Kick-off Pack" - what it will do

Slide 55 / 55 Closing — one problem, three courses, one team◀ 54
Slide 50 / 55 The workshop (1:00–3:00) — Brick 1 “Kick-off Pack”◀ 49 51 ▶

The Brick itself is issued separately on the LMS; this is only a summary of what the two hours produce.

  • 1:00-1:15 - Form teams of two or three (I may balance them); pick a team name; assign a first rotating role: driver (types), navigator (reads and checks), scribe (writes the charter).
  • 1:15-1:45 - Environment check: python --version shows 3.12 or newer; VS Code (Visual Studio Code) with the Python extension; create and activate a virtual environment (python -m venv .venv); write hello_jarvis.py, which prints the team name and the first three rows of boreal_routines_2026.csv with the csv module.
  • 1:45-2:15 - Git and GitHub: create the private team repository from the starter layout (jarvis/, data/, docs/, tests/, analysis/, a .gitignore for Python and .env), a README.md, one commit from every member, and add me as collaborator.
  • 2:15-2:45 - Project Charter, one page in docs/charter.md: team and roles, the business problem in your own words, three questions you would ask the owner, and what "success" looks like on January 22. Start your personal time log in data/timelog_<initials>.csv with today's routines.
  • 2:45-3:00 - Checkpoint (thirty seconds per team): show the README and the running script. Home-work briefing.

Home work (2 h)

Slide 51 / 55 Home work (2 h) and Brick 1 — due Thursday, October 1, 23:59◀ 50 52 ▶
  • Finish Brick 1: charter v1 in the repository; the script runs on every member's machine (one screenshot each).
  • The data diary: log every study and work routine for 14 days - two minutes a day.
  • Read Leedy and Ormrod, Chapter 1, The Nature and Tools of Research (about 40 minutes); note three sentences that define a "research problem".
  • Weekly Progress Report #1 (template on the LMS) - ten minutes.

Brick 1 - Kick-off Pack - due Thursday, October 1, 2026, 23:59 (LMS + GitHub). Deliverables: team repository with README, .gitignore and one commit per member; hello_jarvis.py running on the dataset inside a virtual environment; docs/charter.md (one page); personal time log started (at least five rows per member); Weekly Progress Report #1. Feeds into: the JARVIS repository and README; the technical report's title page, team and first problem statement; your own 14-day dataset (Brick 4).

Team work, submissions and citations: Cyber.SoHo Notice §9 code of ethics, §17 recording and confidentiality of sessions, §18 academic integrity and submitted work, §19 consequences; personal time logs: §6.7, §8.3, §20.
